The Sharptooth tetra Micralestes acutidens is a small-bodied African characid that attains a maximum total length of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters], a modest size that is typical among members of its genus. Field surveys conducted across its range in the Okavango and Zambezi systems indicate that individuals reach their ultimate body mass of 11.2 grams [Wwi = 11.2 grams] only under conditions of high seasonal productivity. This asymptotic mass, derived from length-weight regressions on large series of adults, contrasts notably with the much smaller body sizes reported for congeneric species such as Micralestes humilis. Growth increments in juveniles are strongly linked to the annual flood pulse, with the most rapid size gains occurring during the warm, high-water months when zooplanktonic prey are abundant and temperatures are elevated.

Reproductive development in Micralestes acutidens is characterized by a relatively early onset of puberty, with individuals attaining a total length of 3.4 centimeters [Lp = 3.4 centimeters] at the transition to sexual maturity. At this length, the average wet weight at puberty is 0.55 grams [Wwp = 0.55 grams], a mass that represents only a small fraction of the ultimate adult body size. The initiation of gonadal recrudescence appears to be cued by the rising water temperatures and photoperiod of the early rainy season, a pattern seen in many characiform fishes of southern Africa. Comparative data from related species in the Alestidae suggest that this body size at maturity is relatively low for the family, likely reflecting the selective pressures of a short-lived, fast-paced life history in ephemeral or seasonally fluctuating habitats.

At a stable water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the development of the yolk-sac larva proceeds rapidly, with the chorion rupture and larval eclosion occurring after 6 days [ab = 6 days]. These prolarvae emerge from the incubating egg at a wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], an initial mass that reflects the modest egg diameter of approximately 0.8 millimeters. This minuscule birth mass places the hatchlings firmly within the size range of typical pelagic teleost larvae, where their small body size exposes them to high mortality rates from planktivorous predators during the first days of exogenous feeding. The dependence of embryonic development rate on thermal conditions is pronounced, and the 6-day incubation period observed at 24 °C [T = 24 °C] aligns closely with the predictions of physiological time models for subtropical cypriniforms.

The lifespan of Micralestes acutidens is comparatively brief, with maximum recorded longevity in the wild reaching 1095 days [am = 1095 days] under the thermal regime of natural floodplain environments at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to about three years, is typical for small-bodied characids that occupy seasonally transient habitats and likely reflects high extrinsic mortality rates from piscivorous birds and larger fish. Survivorship curves constructed from mark-recapture data show a steep decline after the second year, with very few individuals persisting beyond their third breeding season. At 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the relatively short potential lifespan constrains the total reproductive window for females, placing a premium on early and efficient allocation to reproduction.

Reproductive output in this species is moderate in magnitude but delivered with high frequency during the wet season. Adult females produce approximately 2 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2 eggs per spawning event], and they can complete up to 350 spawning events each year [F_R_i = up to 350 spawning events each year] when maintained at 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This high spawning frequency compensates for the low fecundity per clutch, enabling a substantial total annual fecundity that is well suited to the unpredictable floodplain environment. The strategy of producing numerous small clutches across an extended breeding season is convergent with that of other iteroparous cypriniforms that face high egg and larval mortality. Gamete release occurs during brief courtship bouts at dawn, and the fertilized ova are broadcast over submerged vegetation.
